title: Window view and relaxation: Viewing green space from a high-rise estate improves urban dwellers' wellbeing
research_focus: To develop a behaviorally and perceptually oriented methodology for the efficient description of environmental geometry and topology, using isovist-based graphs, and to empirically verify its relevance for human spatial behavior and experience.

sample_context.description: 16 participants for rating experiment, 16 participants for navigation experiment, 8 participants for 2D spatial center identification, and 8 additional participants for VR spatial center identification.
sample_context.setting: Virtual gallery rooms and virtual indoor scenes presented via desktop virtual reality (VR) setup or a VR laboratory with headmounted display.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.consequent: Alpha relative power in AF3 (frontal) lobe
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly increased alpha relative power in the AF3 frontal lobe, indicating a state of relaxation and awareness.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.consequent: Alpha relative power in AF4 (frontal) lobe
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly increased alpha relative power in the AF4 frontal lobe, indicating a state of relaxation and awareness.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.consequent: Alpha relative power in O1 (occipital) lobe
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly increased alpha relative power in the O1 occipital lobe, indicating a state of relaxation and awareness.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.consequent: Alpha relative power in O2 (occipital) lobe
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly increased alpha relative power in the O2 occipital lobe, indicating a state of relaxation and awareness.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.consequent: Natural logarithm of high-frequency (HF) power of Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly increased the natural logarithm of high-frequency HRV power, indicating enhanced parasympathetic activity and relaxation.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.consequent: Natural logarithm of low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio of Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly decreased the natural logarithm of the LF/HF ratio, indicating reduced sympathetic nervous activity and stress.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly decreased skin conductance, suggesting reduced psychological stress and arousal.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.consequent: Self-reported 'tension and anxiety', 'fatigue', and 'confusion' mood states (POMS subscales)
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly reduced self-reported feelings of tension and anxiety, fatigue, and confusion.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly increased self-reported vigor.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly lowered the overall Total Mood Disturbance score.

findings.antecedent: Viewing green space from a high-rise window (compared to urban space)
findings.summary: Viewing green space from a high-rise window significantly enhanced positive subjective feelings, making participants feel more comfortable, relaxed, cheerful, beautiful, colorful, and attractive.

derived_hypotheses: Isovist and visibility graph measurands capture behaviorally relevant properties of space, allowing the prediction of affective responses and navigation behavior.
Spatial centers identified by a minimum wall distance algorithm will correspond highly to human-identified spatial centers.
The inclusion of decision points (forks in saddle line skeleton) into place graphs might increase their psychological plausibility for representing space.
Catchment areas associated with each spatial center could correspond to the extent of a space or room.
mechanism_candidates: Affective responses to environments are related to perception via the computational effort required to interpret them or to encode them into spatial memory.
Spatial centers represent positions of balanced perceptual forces, gaining special valence within an environment (Lewin's field theory).
Local distance to spatial boundaries (wall distance) aligns with empirical findings and models of spatial representation in mammal and human brains (place cells, boundary vectors).
Maximizing wall distance implies inscribing circles of maximum size, providing mutual intervisibility and forming regions for communication/interaction (Hillier and Hanson).
transferability_limits: The selected scenes (approx. 90 spaces) are not a representative sample for all architectural environments.
The methodology involves rigorous simplifications, disregarding features like three-dimensional shape, surface properties, presence of other humans/objects, and functional meaning.
The immersive VR interface restricts the field of view (FOV) and introduces viewpoint dependency and influences of exploration.
There is a stronger influence of scale, with centers of small areas tending to be disregarded more often in VR.
The experimental task for center identification did not allow for differentiations between different degrees of center.
The algorithm for center identification weights free-standing columns differently than humans and may miss weak local maxima or centers on long constant saddle lines.
limitations: The analysis involves rigorous simplifications, disregarding features like three-dimensional shape, surface properties, and the presence of other humans or objects and their functional meaning.
The immersive VR interface used in some experiments restricts the FOV and introduces viewpoint dependency and influences of exploration.
The variance in human-identified spatial centers was moderately higher in the VR condition compared to 2D floor plans.
Centers of small areas tended to be disregarded more often in VR, possibly due to absolute scale information provided by the immersive simulation.
The experimental task for center identification did not allow for differentiations between different degrees of center.
The selected granularity of 0.5m for spatial discretization might have side effects, though chosen for parsimony and human locomotion relevance.
The algorithm for identifying spatial centers weights columns differently than humans, sometimes misses weak local maxima, and does not fully capture centers on long constant saddle lines.

paper_metadata.title: From Space Syntax to Space Semantics: A Behaviorally and Perceptually Oriented Methodology for the Efficient Description of the Geometry and Topology of Environments
paper_metadata.journal: Environment and Planning B: Planning and Design
paper_metadata.crossref_title: From Space Syntax to Space Semantics: A Behaviorally and Perceptually Oriented Methodology for the Efficient Description of the Geometry and Topology of Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: Environment and Planning B: Planning and Design
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Human spatial behavior and experience cannot be investigated independently from the shape and configuration of environments. Therefore, comparative studies in architectural psychology and spatial cognition would clearly benefit from operationalizations of space that provide a common denominator for capturing its behavioral and psychologically relevant properties. This paper presents theoretical and methodological issues arising from the practical application of isovist-based graphs for the analysis of architectural spaces. Based on recent studies exploring the influence of spatial form and structure on behavior and experience in virtual environments, the following topics are discussed: (1) the derivation and empirical verification of meaningful descriptor variables on the basis of classic qualitative theories of environmental psychology relating behavior and experience to spatial properties; (2) methods to select reference points for the analysis of architectural spaces at a local level; furthermore, based on two experiments exploring the phenomenal conception of the spatial structure of architectural environments, formalized strategies for (3) the selection of reference points at a global level, and for (4), their integration into a sparse yet plausible comprehensive graph structure, are proposed. Taken together, a well formalized and psychologically oriented methodology for the efficient description of spatial properties of environments at the architectural scale level is outlined. This method appears useful for a wide range of applications, ranging from abstract architectural analysis over behavioral experiments to studies on mental representations in cognitive science.
